question: Which statement best describes linear-gradient?
options: linear-gradient(direction, color stops) paints colors along a straight line. The direction can be an angle (45deg), a keyword (to right, to bottom right), or omitted (defaults to top-to-bottom). It is a background image, so it goes in background or background-image, not background-color.

conic-gradient(from angle at position, stops) sweeps colors around a center point like clock hands. It is the basis for pie charts, color wheels, and progress rings. Repeating variants (repeating-conic-gradient) create pie/checkerboard patterns.

radial-gradient(shape size at position, stops) radiates color outward from a center point in a circle or ellipse. You can control the shape (circle/ellipse), size keywords (closest-side, farthest-corner), and origin (at 30% 30%) — great for spotlights, glows, and soft vignettes.

Stops control where each color sits (0%, 50%, 100%) and how the blend is distributed. Two stops at the same position create a hard edge (a stripe). A single percentage between two colors is a 'color hint' that shifts the midpoint of the blend. Stops are how you make stripes, bands, and precise transitions.
explanation: linear-gradient(direction, color stops) paints colors along a straight line. The direction can be an angle (45deg), a keyword (to right, to bottom right), or omitted (defaults to top-to-bottom). It is a background image, so it goes in background or background-image, not background-color.
